title: Endoscopy: Referral Criteria and Urgent Triggers

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult in a Saudi primary health centre, emergency department or clinic with upper gastrointestinal symptoms (reflux, dyspepsia, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, weight loss, anaemia, bleeding) or lower gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting colorectal cancer: who needs endoscopy, which symptoms trigger an urgent referral, how long to wait, what to do before referral (including stopping acid suppression and a trial of a proton pump inhibitor) and how to safety-net. Uses the 2024 Saudi Gastroenterology Association reflux consensus, a 2025 Riyadh dysphagia referral study and NICE NG12. Not for the endoscopic procedure itself, bowel preparation (see the colonoscopy topic), emergency management of active gastrointestinal bleeding, or children.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health national endoscopy referral guideline was found. The Saudi Gastroenterology Association consensus covers reflux only; the urgent cancer referral rules come from NICE NG12 (England), which has not been validated for Saudi Arabia.

The Riyadh dysphagia study is retrospective, from one centre (168 patients, 2022 to 2023), measures improvement by patient report and shows an association, not proof, that endoscopy within 2 weeks helps.

Age thresholds (55 and over for upper gastrointestinal cancer, 40, 50 and 60 for colorectal) are English thresholds; local cancer incidence by age in Saudi Arabia was not checked and no local threshold is written.

The consensus says to stop a proton pump inhibitor for at least 2 weeks before endoscopy only for unproven reflux; whether to stop it before endoscopy for other indications (for example bleeding, suspected cancer) and how to bridge severe symptoms was not specified in numbers beyond that and is left to the endoscopist.

Management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, antithrombotic management before endoscopy and sedation and anaesthesia are not in the sources read, so no regimen is written; see the bleeding and colonoscopy topics.
Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, and testing for coeliac disease, were not in the sources read, so they are not written as steps; check a local protocol.

Faecal immunochemical test cut-off (10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces) and the test brands are from NICE NG12 and the availability of those tests in Saudi primary care was not checked; Saudi Ministry of Health colorectal screening is covered in the colonoscopy topic.

The consensus recommends a 6 to 8 week standard-dose proton pump inhibitor trial; the omeprazole label allows up to 4 weeks for symptomatic reflux (8 weeks for erosive oesophagitis) and the pantoprazole label covers short-term treatment of erosive oesophagitis for up to 8 weeks only; the two labels and the consensus differ and the clinician must choose and document.
Potassium-competitive acid blockers are named in the consensus as an alternative where available, but no dose was read and none is written.
Figures were read by automated extraction of article, guideline and label text; spot-check each figure and dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: Endoscopy lets the doctor see and biopsy the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum, so it can find cancer, ulcer, oesophagitis, Barrett's oesophagus and other causes that symptoms and drugs cannot separate (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy). Alarm symptoms (dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia, gastrointestinal bleeding) point to structural disease including cancer and call for endoscopy as the first step, not a drug trial (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 6). A symptomatic response to a proton pump inhibitor does not exclude gastric cancer, so early relapse or poor response needs further testing and, in older adults, endoscopy (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.1 Presence of Gastric Malignancy). Stopping the proton pump inhibitor for 2 weeks before endoscopy for unproven reflux avoids masking oesophagitis and eosinophilic oesophagitis (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 7 and Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy). Dysphagia is common (about 3% of adults) and most causes are benign, but malignancy was found in 6.5% of Riyadh referrals and 67% of those worsened (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Introduction and Section Results).

symptoms: Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), food sticking, painful swallowing (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Introduction).
Heartburn and regurgitation, chest pain on eating, globus sensation (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results).
Unintentional weight loss, vomiting, upper abdominal pain, dyspepsia (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1 and Recommendation 1.2.9).
Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding or abdominal pain with weight loss (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.1).
physicalSigns: Pallor or low haemoglobin on blood testing (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.9 and Recommendation 1.3.1).
Jaundice in a person aged 40 or over (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.4).
Abdominal or rectal mass (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.1).
redFlags: Dysphagia at any age: refer on a suspected cancer pathway; endoscopy within 2 weeks gave better outcomes in a Riyadh cohort (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1; Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Conclusion).
Aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia: suspected cancer referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1 and Recommendation 1.2.7).
Haematemesis: consider direct-access endoscopy (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.2 and Recommendation 1.2.8). Active or heavy bleeding is an emergency; send to hospital.
Jaundice in a person aged 40 or over: suspected cancer referral for pancreatic cancer (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.4).
Faecal immunochemical test result of 10 micrograms haemoglobin per gram of faeces or more: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.2).
Anaemia, abdominal mass, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding with weight loss or pain: offer a faecal immunochemical test and refer according to the result (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.1).
precipitants: Age above 50, male sex, hiatal hernia and obesity raise the risk of Barrett's oesophagus and strengthen the case for endoscopy when several are present (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1: Clinical assessment and response to PPI therapy).
Persistent symptoms despite optimal proton pump inhibitor treatment (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).
Reflux complications such as stricture, Barrett's oesophagus or adenocarcinoma (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).
Suspected reflux-related extraesophageal symptoms such as cough or asthma (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Heartburn and regurgitation, most common cause of dysphagia referral (45.2%); proven only by endoscopy or pH monitoring (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 1).

14.8% of dysphagia referrals; can be masked by a proton pump inhibitor, so biopsy when suspected (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).
Dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus pain, reflux or dyspepsia; malignancy 6.5% of dysphagia referrals (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1; Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results).
Regurgitation with negative endoscopy and pH monitoring; confirmed by high-resolution manometry (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 12).
Change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding, anaemia, abdominal mass, weight loss; faecal immunochemical test 10 micrograms per gram or more (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.1 and Recommendation 1.3.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Look for alarm features and emergencies
actions: Ask about difficulty swallowing, weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools, jaundice, bowel habit change and rectal bleeding (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1: Clinical assessment and response to PPI therapy).
Send immediately to hospital if there is active or heavy bleeding; that is an emergency and not a referral (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.2).
Take a history of obesity, hiatal hernia, age over 50 and male sex as Barrett's risks (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1: Clinical assessment and response to PPI therapy).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer urgently when triggers are present
actions: Refer on a suspected cancer pathway for dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1 and Recommendation 1.2.7).
Refer jaundiced people aged 40 and over (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.4).
Prioritise endoscopy within 2 weeks for dysphagia; delays over 2 weeks affected 44% for assessment and 50% for endoscopy in Riyadh (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results).
Use a direct referral pathway rather than a general clinic first (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Conclusion).

clinicalManagement.title: Consider direct-access endoscopy
actions: Consider non-urgent endoscopy for haematemesis, or age 55 and over with treatment-resistant dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin, raised platelets or nausea and vomiting with other symptoms (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.3 and Recommendation 1.2.9).
Check a full blood count first (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Trial of acid suppression for classic symptoms without alarm features
actions: Give a standard-dose proton pump inhibitor for 6 to 8 weeks (see medicines) (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4).
Advise weight loss, avoiding meals 3 to 4 hours before bed, raising the head of the bed and stopping smoking and alcohol (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Lifestyle modifications).
Stop the drug or use the lowest effective dose if the response is good (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4).

Do not rely on a good response to exclude cancer; refer for endoscopy if the response is poor or symptoms relapse early (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.1 Presence of Gastric Malignancy; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1.3: Role of PPI testing).

clinicalManagement.title: Prepare for endoscopy
actions: For unproven reflux, stop the proton pump inhibitor for at least 2 weeks before upper endoscopy; balance this against rebound symptoms in severe cases (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 7 and Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).
Request biopsies for dysphagia, chest pain on eating, suspected eosinophilic oesophagitis or Barrett's oesophagus (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 2.1: Upper GI endoscopy).
Ask the endoscopist to grade oesophagitis with the Los Angeles classification and Barrett's oesophagus with the Prague classification (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 8).

clinicalManagement.title: Handle lower gastrointestinal symptoms
actions: Offer a quantitative faecal immunochemical test for abdominal mass, change in bowel habit, anaemia, or age-related weight loss, pain or bleeding (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.1).

Refer on a suspected cancer pathway at a result of 10 micrograms per gram or more; keep safety-netting for lower results or unreturned samples (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.2 and Recommendation 1.3.3).

clinicalManagement.title: Safety-net and follow up
actions: Review people who do not meet referral criteria but have symptoms linked with cancer, and arrange a recheck (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1 to Recommendation 1.3.3).
Record the date of referral, the target date for endoscopy and the result (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Conclusion).

regimens.indication: Symptomatic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease without alarm features
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with classic reflux symptoms and no alarm features
regimens.dose: 20 mg once daily (Omeprazole label, Dosage and Administration, Table 1: treatment of symptomatic GERD). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow the capsule whole, do not chew; if unable to swallow, open the capsule and give the microtablets in one tablespoon of cool, soft applesauce, swallowed immediately with cool water, without chewing or crushing (Omeprazole label, Administration Instructions).
regimens.route: Oral, before a meal (Omeprazole label, Administration Instructions)
regimens.frequency: Once daily; if a dose is missed take it as soon as possible, but never take two doses at once (Omeprazole label, Administration Instructions)
regimens.duration: Up to 4 weeks on the label for symptomatic reflux, and 4 to 8 weeks for erosive oesophagitis; the Saudi consensus recommends 6 to 8 weeks, then stop or use the lowest effective dose (Omeprazole label, Table 1; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4)
adjustments: Hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A, B or C) and Asian patients: reduce to 10 mg once daily for maintenance of healing (Omeprazole label, Dosage and Administration, footnote and Section 8.6).
Avoid with clopidogrel because omeprazole reduces its active metabolite (Omeprazole label, Section 5.7).
Avoid with CYP2C19 or CYP3A4 inducers such as rifampin and St John's wort (Omeprazole label, Section 5.9).
Symptomatic response does not exclude gastric malignancy (Omeprazole label, Section 5.1).
Pregnancy: the Saudi consensus states that proton pump inhibitors except omeprazole are considered safe in pregnancy (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 22).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Response at 6 to 8 weeks; poor response or early relapse needs endoscopy (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1.3: Role of PPI testing).
Diarrhoea with fever or blood: consider Clostridioides difficile infection (Omeprazole label, Section 5.3).
Long-term use: magnesium, vitamin B12 and bone fracture risk (Omeprazole label, Warnings and Precautions).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to omeprazole, any substituted benzimidazole or the formulation (Omeprazole label, Contraindications).
Treatment with a rilpivirine-containing product (Omeprazole label, Contraindications).

regimens.indication: Gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms in an adult without alarm features (label indication is erosive oesophagitis)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with classic reflux symptoms and no alarm features
regimens.dose: 40 mg once daily (Pantoprazole label, Dosage and Administration, Table 1: short-term treatment of erosive oesophagitis associated with GERD). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow the tablet whole, do not split, chew or crush (Pantoprazole label, Administration Instructions).
regimens.route: Oral, with or without food (Pantoprazole label, Administration Instructions)
regimens.duration: Up to 8 weeks on the label for erosive oesophagitis; the Saudi consensus recommends 6 to 8 weeks, then stop or use the lowest effective dose (Pantoprazole label, Table 1; Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4)
adjustments: Hepatic impairment: exposure rises (AUC 5- to 7-fold in cirrhosis) so review the dose and indication (Pantoprazole label, Section 12.3).
Methotrexate (mainly at high dose): proton pump inhibitors may raise methotrexate levels (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.13).
Atazanavir and other antiretrovirals: effect variable; see the antiretroviral label (Pantoprazole label, Drug Interactions).
Symptomatic response does not exclude gastric malignancy; consider endoscopy in older patients with poor response (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Response at 6 to 8 weeks (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4).
Persistent diarrhoea: Clostridioides difficile (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.3).
Long-term use: fracture risk and low magnesium (Pantoprazole label, Section 5.4 and Section 5.8).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to any component or any substituted benzimidazole (Pantoprazole label, Contraindications).
Treatment with a rilpivirine-containing product (Pantoprazole label, Contraindications).

branches.label: Trial of acid suppression for classic reflux symptoms without alarm features
branches.entryCriteria: Adult with classic heartburn or regurgitation, no dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia, bleeding or other alarm feature, no rilpivirine treatment, no known allergy to a substituted benzimidazole.

medicationPlan.note: A proton pump inhibitor is the only medicine in this pathway: the empirical trial for classic reflux symptoms in an adult without alarm features. One of two is chosen. The consensus recommends a 6 to 8 week standard-dose trial without naming a drug or dose; doses, administration and cautions are taken from the product labels. Both labels differ from the consensus on duration (see unverified). All doses are for adults. SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia; or multiple risk factors for Barrett's oesophagus (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 6).

Classic reflux symptoms and no alarm features: 6 to 8 weeks of standard-dose proton pump inhibitor, then stop or use the lowest effective dose if there is a good response (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Statement 4).
Suboptimal response, early relapse or persistent symptoms despite optimal therapy (Saudi Gastroenterology Association GERD consensus, Step 1.3: Role of PPI testing).
Endoscopy within 2 weeks for dysphagia: 84.6% improved with endoscopy within 2 weeks compared with 76.0% with delay (Riyadh dysphagia study, Section Results).
Dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.1).

Haematemesis; or age 55 and over with treatment-resistant dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin, raised platelets with nausea, vomiting, weight loss, reflux, dyspepsia or pain, or nausea or vomiting with weight loss, reflux, dyspepsia or pain (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.2.3 and Recommendation 1.2.9).
Faecal immunochemical test result of 10 micrograms haemoglobin per gram of faeces or more: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12, Recommendation 1.3.2).

teaching.scope: Adult in a Saudi primary health centre, emergency department or clinic with upper gastrointestinal symptoms (reflux, dyspepsia, difficulty swallowing, vomiting, weight loss, anaemia, bleeding) or lower gastrointestinal symptoms suggesting colorectal cancer: who needs endoscopy, which symptoms trigger an urgent referral, how long to wait, what to do before referral (including stopping acid suppression and a trial of a proton pump inhibitor) and how to safety-net. Uses the 2024 Saudi Gastroenterology Association reflux consensus, a 2025 Riyadh dysphagia referral study and NICE NG12. Not for the endoscopic procedure itself, bowel preparation (see the colonoscopy topic), emergency management of active gastrointestinal bleeding, or children.
learningObjectives: Send people with alarm features straight to endoscopy.
Aim for endoscopy within 2 weeks for dysphagia.
Use a 6 to 8 week proton pump inhibitor trial only when there are no alarm features.
Stop the drug 2 weeks before endoscopy for unproven reflux.
pitfalls: Treating dysphagia with a drug trial.
Staying on a proton pump inhibitor without review.
Forgetting to stop the drug before endoscopy for unproven reflux.
keyPoints: A good response to a proton pump inhibitor does not exclude cancer.
Delays beyond 2 weeks were common in Riyadh.
Haematemesis or heavy bleeding is an emergency.
A negative faecal immunochemical test needs safety-netting if concern persists.

patientEducation: Endoscopy is a camera test that looks at the food pipe and stomach and can take small samples.
Tell us at once if swallowing is getting harder, you are losing weight without trying, you vomit blood or pass black stools.
Acid-reducing medicine can relieve heartburn, but a good response does not mean there is no serious cause.
If a test of your stool for blood is positive, you will be referred quickly for a camera test of the bowel.
Stop acid-reducing medicine for 2 weeks before the camera test only if your doctor tells you to.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid large meals within 3 to 4 hours of bedtime.
Raise the head of the bed.
Reduce your own trigger foods rather than avoiding long lists.
mdtReferrals: Primary care physician; gastroenterologist or endoscopist; endoscopy nurse; pathologist; surgeon or oncologist for cancer pathway; dietitian for swallowing and weight loss; radiologist.
dischargeCriteria: Date of referral and target date for endoscopy recorded; interim advice on warning signs; proton pump inhibitor plan before the test; plan if the result is normal or abnormal.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review 6 to 8 weeks after starting a proton pump inhibitor and refer for endoscopy if the response is poor or symptoms relapse early; follow up urgent referrals until the endoscopy result is received.
